Commentary by a Member of the Foundation for Psychotherapy and Counselling, and the Circle of Analytical Psychology, London

Jonathan Barham

Jonathan Barham

[jonathanbarham@yahoo.co.uk]

Jonathan Barham  

I much appreciated reading about Pauline and her therapist, and I am grateful to them for their generosity in providing the material. I would like to comment around a couple of areas of significance that have emerged: the idea of therapy as adventure, and the development of therapeutic trust.

A patient once told me that the Latin root for adventure (advenir = to arrive, come to) originally had a military meaning to do with being ‘in the thick of it’; for example, coming to the foot of the walls of a citadel which is about to be stormed. True or not etymologically, it is this word and image which has presented itself to me in response to Pauline and her therapist's story.

There is an obvious analogy here with Pauline in her citadel room. However, the image of Pauline and her therapist up close to the walls of a citadel is also an image of the defences against relating to each other and to others more fully - the heart, as it were, of the therapeutic task and adventure. These defences are there to prevent undeveloped sides and unassimilable experiences coming to the fore - in Pauline's case, for example, needy, vulnerable, shadowy-aggressive aspects of herself. They are automatically treated as toxic and threatening to the conscious personality in its relations both internally and with others.

Analytic psychotherapy is built on our own personal experience of the good enough therapeutic environment allowing habitually suppressed or undeveloped forms of relating and bad experiences to be sympathetically (gk sym = together; pathos = feeling) engaged with and met. In this way the old limiting and isolating states can break down, thereby allowing new ones to emerge in the form of learnt experience. Pauline presents with depression and anxiety but has to keep the therapist ‘at a distance’ from them. Depression and anxiety are abstract (i.e. non-sympathetic) attempts to name and relate to these old states. She comes in the hope of them being given meaning and life through analytic - sympathetic - attention. Her depressed state, a hidden lack of aliveness from which the therapist is distanced, has foundations in raw suppressed emotions that have been rendered undeveloped and unavailable through the lack of a more integrated and benign internal parental couple. Pauline's actual parents, from which her internal couple are derived, were at the very least preoccupied with the disabled sibling and clearly had other relational impasses to contend with too. There was probably not much in their parenting to give her an experience of being able to work through difficulties. Pauline's anxiety could therefore be seen as stemming from having little idea about what to do with any raw emotions - for example desire, alarm, helplessness and anger, threatening to manifest in a relationship.

Commentary by a Member of the British Psychotherapy Foundation, London

Annie Pesskin

Annie Pesskin

[annie.pesskin@gmail.com]

Annie Pesskin  

In this commentary, I thought it would be interesting to offer a neuropsychoanalytic perspective on the clinical material. Neuropsychoanalysis is an attempt to think bilingually - a yoking together of neurological ways of understanding the brain with psychoanalytic ideas about the mind. It may be useful to consider the clinical implications of thinking in this way when considering the material provided.

When presented with clinical material, there are four questions to ask about the patient in order to work neuropsychoanalytically. I will therefore ask each question in turn and attempt to offer as full an answer as I can.

Question 1 - What Feeling Does the Patient Suffer From?

Pauline appears to suffer predominantly from PANIC/GRIEF but I think it would be fair to say there is probably some FEAR and RAGE mixed in there too. (I italicize these affects as they refer specifically to three of Jaak Panksaap's seven Basic Affects, the other four being LUST, CARE, PLAY and SEEKING.)

Another way of answering this question is to ask which need is currently not being met? I think it is the need to feel safe with someone and to be able to rely on them. Both Pauline's history and also her behaviour in the reported session would suggest this is problematic for her.

Question 2 - What Unconscious Prediction Does the Patient Use to Meet that Need? (This is Enacted in ‘the Transference’, Broadly Defined)

Neuropsychoanalysis makes the assumption that the problems we encounter in our relationships recur because they are automatized solutions to problems we encountered early on in our lives. They are automatized solutions because they were effective in coping with conflictual emotional experiences in the past and they have become unconscious ways of relating. As they are unconscious, we are not aware we are using these ‘solutions’ to predict the way others will treat us. But we do.

In Pauline's case, she uses the unconscious prediction that she will be left to solve her uncertainty about whether or not she is being left. When she was little, she was left to fend for herself because her disabled sibling took up all the mother's bandwidth and Pauline's father was too abusive/angry to step into the breach.

The Knitting Knows: On Learning How to Work with the Countertransference

Kylie Innocente

Kylie Innocente

[kylie@innocentemail.com]

Kylie Innocente   Third year psychoanalytic psychotherapy trainee at the New South Wales Institute of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (NSWIPP), Sydney, Australia. She currently works in Perinatal Infant Mental Health at the North Sydney Local Health District and in private practice based in St Leonards, Sydney. She received her degree in occupational therapy from La Trobe University, Melbourne and her MSc from Kings College London, with research into dynamic psychotherapy, anthropology, and the history of psychiatry. Her clinical experience includes community mental health, addictions, youth mental health, inpatient therapies, mental health rehabilitation and perinatal infant mental health.
Countertransference, Projective Identification, Knitting, Infant Observation, Supervision

Learning how to identify and work with the countertransference is a cornerstone of any psychoanalytic training, yet it can't be taught solely through books or in the classroom. Experience of the countertransference and having it pointed out through supervision or a peer group is an essential component of this learning process. Nonetheless, countertransference can be missed as it's often an unconscious form of communication. This article explores, through the example of an infant observation, how an intense countertransference penetrated unchecked and unnoticed but was enacted through the creative act of knitting. The emergence of this countertransference is examined and is then considered through the lens of a ‘creative block’. This idea gives a different way to think about unconscious processes and enriches the understanding of what is being communicated.

PSYCHOANALYSIS, DEATH DRIVE/INSTINCT, PATHOLOGICAL ORGANIZATION, TERMINATION OF TREATMENT, CLINICAL PRACTICE

The paper describes an analysis with a very difficult, emotionally inaccessible patient who, after more than a year, unexpectedly terminated the analysis, leaving the analyst with a sense of frustration due to incomplete and interrupted analysis. In the theoretical section of the paper, the author presents his understanding of the creation of such a pathological organization, starting with Freud's concept of death drive, then going on to Melanie Klein's and her successor's discoveries. John Steiner's concept of ‘psychic retreat’ helps us to understand the process of development of a pathological organization of personality. In the last part, the author describes how he works through mourning and prompts reflection on the reasons for the premature termination of the treatment by the patient. He indicates the causes in both the patient and the analyst.

The Experience of Time Boundaries in Remote Working

Sue Kegerreis

Sue Kegerreis

skeger@essex.ac.uk

Sue Kegerreis   Professor at the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies at the University of Essex. As a psychotherapist (both child/adolescent and adult) she has practised in health, education and community settings as well as in private practice. She established the MSc Psychodynamic Counselling with Children and Adolescents at Birkbeck and the MA Psychodynamic Counselling at the University of Essex. She has also taught on numerous other psychotherapy and counselling trainings. She has published widely in professional journals, is Managing Editor of Psychodynamic Practice and her book Psychodynamic Counselling with Children and Adolescents was published in 2010.
TIME BOUNDARIES, REMOTE WORKING, COVID 19 PANDEMIC, PSYCHOANALYTIC SETTING, LATENESS

In this paper I consider the experiences around the time boundary of therapeutic sessions of both therapists and patients working remotely during the pandemic. I discuss the precision of electronic time and the different dynamics around the beginning of sessions. The business of arriving, whether early, on time or late, has different drivers and meanings in the online world. I consider how difficult it is to take up these dynamics adequately when faced with the real uncertainties of internet connections. Communications between therapist and patient around time boundaries have also presented new challenges, and the way sessions end is very different. The experience of time within sessions is altered, and sessions are no longer bracketed with the journey to and from the consulting room. The dynamics around power and vulnerability are different and the management of time boundaries bring these dynamics vividly to life. The paper closes with some practical considerations around remote working as this is likely to be a part of our practice even after the pandemic is finally over.

Rozsika Parker Prize 2022

The British Journal of Psychotherapy‘s Prize established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker focuses on a critical engagement with psychoanalysis and questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should consult the BJP‘s submission guidelines, particularly in relation to confidentiality and consent. Any clinical material must be fully anonymized, with disguise of any biographical details. The work should be prepared with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student Path is open to students on an initial training leading to a clinical qualification: this may be in psychodynamic counselling, psychodynamic psychotherapy, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, psychoanalytic child psychotherapy, group analysis, psychoanalysis or clinical or counselling psychology. Student entrants may be currently in training or have qualified within the last 12 months. The Student Path is also open to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. The Post-Qualification Path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers (Student or Post-Qualification) may have been submitted as part of the requirements of a programme of study, if this is acceptable to the author's course team, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. A maximum of 4 illustrations is permitted, and the author must obtain permission to use them if they are not the author's own work. The word length must be stated on the title page. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i.e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to The Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

A.H. Brafman: 1931-2022

Brett Kahr

Brett Kahr

[kahr14@aol.com]

Brett Kahr  

On 31 January 2022, Dr Abrahão Henrique Brafman, one of the United Kingdom's most admired child psychiatrists and psychoanalysts, passed away at the age of 90 years, after having enjoyed a distinguished career as a clinician, a teacher, and an author, as well as a much appreciated colleague to innumerable individuals, all of whom benefited from his wide-ranging wisdom.

Born on 8 April 1931, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Abrahão Brafman, known more familiarly as ‘Abe’, studied medicine in his native country, and then, in 1959, emigrated to London. Not long thereafter, he became a candidate at the Institute of Psycho-Analysis, and, after having pursued a five-times-weekly training analysis with Dr Paula Heimann, as well as clinical supervision from Dr Michael Balint, Dr Lois Munro, Mrs Eva Rosenfeld, and Dr Hanna Segal, he qualified in 1964.

Across his long career, Brafman served as a Consultant Psychiatrist in the National Health Service, specializing in child and adolescent psychiatry. Over the years, Abe worked in a range of institutions, such as Queen Mary's Hospital, in Roehampton, in South West London, where he ran groups for under-fives and their parents, as well as University College Hospital in Central London, where, as an Honorary Senior Clinical Lecturer, he introduced medical students to psychoanalytical concepts.

After Brafman retired from his many decades in the public sector, he expanded his private psychoanalytical practice in Hampstead, in North West London, and facilitated his clinical work with such reliability and professionalism that large numbers of patients yearned for appointments. Over the years, I referred many people to Dr Brafman, all of whom spoke with tremendous appreciation for the kindly and sensible way in which he engaged with their narratives of pain and distress.

Brafman will be best remembered for his extensive writing career, having first published in the English language while still in his 30s and having continued to do so until his final years. The sheer range of Brafman's essays and book chapters can only be described as impressive, including contributions on such diverse topics as student mental health, psychosomatic medicine, infant observation, countertransfer-ence, suicidality, retirement, and so many more. Brafman also published a handful of engaging books for both mental health colleagues, and also, for parents. I particularly recommend his much-admired tome, Untying the Knot: Working with Children and Parents, in which he championed Dr Donald Winnicott's concept of the therapeutic consultation and the vital role of the squiggle technique and other forms of drawing in the facilitation of communication with young people.

Estela Welldon Prize 2022

The British Journal of Psychotherapy is delighted to invite entries for the 2022 Estela Welldon Prize. Dr Estela V. Welldon worked for 40 years at the Portman Clinic in London as Consultant Psychiatrist and Consultant Psychotherapist. She is the Founder and Honorary President for Life of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, which, since its foundation, has held professional meetings every year in different parts of the world. Dr Welldon is the author, among many other works, of Mother, Madonna, Whore: The Idealization and Denigration of Motherhood, which challenged the traditional psychoanalytic theory that perversions are unique to males and which exposed the nature of female sexual offending. Creator of the world's first ever training course in forensic psychotherapy, in collaboration with the medical school at University College London, she has worked as both an individual and group practitioner for decades and continues to do so.

‘As a psychiatrist’, Dr Welldon has written, ‘I have spent my time contemplating the depths of the human psyche - sometimes in despair but usually in wonderment. As a forensic psychotherapist, I have continually been drawn to “the beauty hidden within the ugly”.’ She has often stated that every practitioner must search for the “golden nugget” of goodness and approachability within every patient, even those who seem unapproachable, such as certain forensic patients. The Prize, which is co-sponsored by the BJP and the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy and was initiated in 2021, will be awarded annually to the author of a paper which contributes to our understanding of the shadow side of human nature - the ugly side, or what we might previously have called the ‘dark side’ of humanity. This might refer to acts of forensic violence, or cruelty in more intimate contexts. The Prize will be given to the paper which both illuminates the nature of human psychopathology in this area, and which reveals how the analytic clinician can overcome the obstacles and the challenges of therapeutic work to find that golden nugget.

[[RunningHead]]

Rozsika Parker Prize 2022

The British Journal of Psychotherapy‘s Prize established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker focuses on a critical engagement with psychoanalysis and questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should consult the BJP‘s submission guidelines, particularly in relation to confidentiality and consent. Any clinical material must be fully anonymized, with disguise of any biographical details. The work should be prepared with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student Path is open to students on an initial training leading to a clinical qualification: this may be in psychodynamic counselling, psychodynamic psychotherapy, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, psychoanalytic child psychotherapy, group analysis, psychoanalysis or clinical or counselling psychology. Student entrants may be currently in training or have qualified within the last 12 months. The Student Path is also open to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. The Post-Qualification Path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers (Student or Post-Qualification) may have been submitted as part of the requirements of a programme of study, if this is acceptable to the author's course team, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. A maximum of 4 illustrations is permitted, and the author must obtain permission to use them if they are not the author's own work. The word length must be stated on the title page. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i.e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to The Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

[[RunningHead]]

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

In last November's issue of the Journal, I announced that I would be retiring as Editor-in-Chief of the BJP this summer, after twelve years in post, and said that in a future editorial I would ‘reflect further on the work and on the Journal's project, and acknowledge the many colleagues who have worked with me, and guided me, over this time’ (Scott, 2021, p.547). The interview with me which opens this issue of the Journal, my last, has given me a wonderful opportunity to reflect on the work and on the Journal's project, in an in-depth conversation with our colleague Brett Kahr. I am grateful to Brett for suggesting the interview, and grateful to the Editorial Board, who put forward a range of questions for me to respond to, which Brett then shaped editorially. It has been very rewarding for me to consider the Journal's project from these different but related perspectives, and I hope the interview will be of interest to readers in presenting and reflecting on my sense of that project.

When I took up the editorship in 2009, the Journal had been in print for twenty-five years. My aim, as in any established publishing project, was both to consolidate and to innovate. In doing so I have relied on the Journal's authors to work with us in both areas, and I have been impressed by their ongoing engagement with the task. More generally, I want to acknowledge the invaluable guidance and support I have received in relation to both parts of the work. I have written elsewhere of my enduring debt to Bob Hinshelwood, the Journal's founder and first Editor. For the project as a whole, there are too many people to name individually, but they are all in my mind as I write. The Journal is co-owned by the British Psychotherapy Foundation and Wiley, and I have at all times been able to rely on their advice and involvement - as colleagues and as owners - in developing the Journal both practically and strategically. I have worked closely with the Editorial Board throughout my time in post, not just in relation to the assessment of manuscripts - though that is an important part of their work - but in discussing the many topics which any Journal has to consider: How might we develop our work? Did we get this right? Did we miss something? What needs rethinking? What is new in the field? How should we approach a certain theme' I was able to ask the Board - through its various changes of membership - the question that mattered to me most: ‘What do you think?’. I knew that there would be a prompt and ready response to each question, and that it would be the range of views expressed that would enable us to funnel down to what felt the right course of action, the right decision.

Editor's Comments

Gary Winship

Gary Winship

Gary.winship@nottingham.ac.uk

Gary Winship  

In line with the joint strategy plan between the British Psychotherapy Foundation and Wiley, my vision for the journal is to ensure that it remains a highly prestigious and indispensable psychotherapy practitioner journal that continues to bring together colleagues working across inclusive pluralistic psychoanalytic traditions. There is a lack of recognition for the considerable work that thousands of psychoanalytic psychotherapy colleagues, working outside of core state services, deliver for the betterment of the mental health of the nation. The impact of this work is often understated, under recognized and under resourced. But high calibre papers, single case studies, add to what Mike Rustin (1997) calls a critical mass of qualitative research opinion (‘Give me a consulting room and I will raise you the world’). Thereafter this critical mass of evidence can start to shape policy. The British Journal of Psychotherapy is perfectly placed as a champion of generating evidence, ensuring that the impact of psychoanalytic psychotherapy is esteemed and positioned accordingly, maximizing the benefit for clients.

Psychotherapists often have a self-consciousness about doing research, but in reality it is a question of narrative finesse in articulating the value of qualitative case study approaches that are at the heart of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy reflective practice. One of the areas I am keen to see is collaborative writing sitting alongside the tradition of single authored papers in psychotherapy. As editor, I want to take the opportunity, where I can, to connect people together, building and nurturing networks of authors who have shared interests, working with organizations, using some of my time running writing workshops and encouraging submissions from early career practitioners. Alongside my practice as a psychotherapist I am also well positioned as a University of Nottingham academic to attend conferences, both in the UK and overseas, meeting stakeholders and sharing the valuable work of the journal.

[[RunningHead]]

Estela Welldon Prize 2022

The British Journal of Psychotherapy is delighted to invite entries for the 2022 Estela Welldon Prize. Dr Estela V. Welldon worked for 40 years at the Portman Clinic in London as Consultant Psychiatrist and Consultant Psychotherapist. She is the Founder and Honorary President for Life of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, which, since its foundation, has held professional meetings every year in different parts of the world. Dr Welldon is the author, among many other works, of Mother, Madonna, Whore: The Idealization and Denigration of Motherhood, which challenged the traditional psychoanalytic theory that perversions are unique to males and which exposed the nature of female sexual offending. Creator of the world's first ever training course in forensic psychotherapy, in collaboration with the medical school at University College London, she has worked as both an individual and group practitioner for decades and continues to do so.

‘As a psychiatrist’, Dr Welldon has written, ‘I have spent my time contemplating the depths of the human psyche — sometimes in despair but usually in wonderment. As a forensic psychotherapist, I have continually been drawn to “the beauty hidden within the ugly”.’ She has often stated that every practitioner must search for the “golden nugget” of goodness and approachability within every patient, even those who seem unapproachable, such as certain forensic patients. The Prize, which is co-sponsored by the BJP and the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy and was initiated in 2021, will be awarded annually to the author of a paper which contributes to our understanding of the shadow side of human nature — the ugly side, or what we might previously have called the ‘dark side’ of humanity. This might refer to acts of forensic violence, or cruelty in more intimate contexts. The Prize will be given to the paper which both illuminates the nature of human psychopathology in this area, and which reveals how the analytic clinician can overcome the obstacles and the challenges of therapeutic work to find that golden nugget.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

It is always a pleasure to announce the winning and commended authors in the Rozsika Parker Prize in the May issue of the Journal. The 2021 submissions were strongly international, in both Student and Post-Qualification paths, as readers will see from the announcement on the next page - a testament to the increasing reach and standing of the Prize. The winning papers in both categories will be published in the August issue, and the four commended papers - two in each path - will be published in the November issue.

There is much to savour in this issue. Our Clinical Commentary looks in granular detail at a treatment that is finally able to move ‘from Zoom to the room’, as Katya Orrell puts it. Heather Wood's commended 2021 Estela Welldon paper presents a seven-year analytic treatment illustrating Wood's formulation of a ‘paedophilic breakdown’ as distinct from enduring paedophilia. In our New Voices strand, Lorraine Vivian explores the creation of a primary imago from a Winnicottian perspective. In our Clinical and Theoretical Practice strand, Stephen Blumenthal looks at the imbalance between maternal and paternal functions in situations of compulsive sexual behaviour. Marcus Evans then explores the development of a trans identity ‘in defence against an underlying fear of depressive anxieties and psychic collapse’. Next, David Mann introduces the ‘Nice But Boring Object’ - a rejected relationship - in the context of ‘earlier experiences of a sterile or depressed relationship with an unavailable primary care giver’. And Damian McCann explores the complexity involved in undertaking couple therapy in the presence of only one of the partners.

We return, as so often, to Covid. Sari Goldstein Ferber and Aron Weller term the electronic device ‘the inanimate third’ in the therapeutic process. Ivan Shanley, Claire Jones and Neelima Reddi report on core psychiatry training during the pandemic, in which psychodynamic psychotherapy was delivered by phone, allowing trainees to achieve required competencies.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

As readers will know, the Journal's annual Prize in honour of the psychiatrist and forensic psychotherapist Estela Welldon was established a year ago. It is awarded to ‘the author of a paper which contributes to our understanding of the shadow side of human nature’. We are delighted that in its first year, we have joint winners and a commended author. The winning papers, both offering rich accounts of the clinical encounter, are published in this issue of the journal. First, Stephen Blumenthal considers the challenges of working with a psychic retreat based upon disavowal. ‘A state of inbetweenness’, he suggests, ‘protects the person from knowing about their aggressive impulses, their need for care and the passing of time’. Two parallel worlds existed, ‘one in which [my patient S] was omnipotent, and the other in which he needed and depended on others. These worlds began to collide and S was able to communicate to me that. …I should not mistake his apparent self-containment for self-sufficiency’. Then, Elena Mundici considers the relationship between music and violence. ‘Similarly to violence’, she writes, ‘the execution of a piece of music involves a synergy of physical, mental and affective functions, and an interaction of conscious and unconscious forces.’ Noting that ‘the structured and formal language of music provided a rigorous yet flexible space where [a] prisoner's internal world and unconscious phantasies could begin to be confronted’, she explores how piano training provided a dimension where creativity and destructiveness could be enacted ‘without fatal consequences’.

Heather Wood's commended paper will be published in our May issue. Our congratulations again to all three authors.

In our New Voices strand, Susan Tyler explores substance misuse problems among children of alcoholics (COAs), from the perspective of transgenerational trauma. There is a particular focus on Jung's concept of the transcendent function, which provides, the author suggests, ‘a powerful therapeutic tool to link divided and split off parts of the self in a containing matrix’. The paper is vividly illustrated with the case of a female patient who had been ‘sober for 12 years and was not actively drinking when we began the work’. Even so, ‘her internal world retained the addictive features common to COAs’.

Hester Mcfarland Solomon 1943 - 2021

Ann Kutek

Ann Kutek

[qt@clara.net]

Ann Kutek  

Hester McFarland Solomon, who died on 5 October 2021 aged 78, was an American émigré who made a felicitous choice of life partner and adopted the UK as her home. It also proved to be the locus where her early dreams about travel, philosophy and Carl Jung became realized. Albeit a French graduate, her transition from home-maker and mother to sought-after analyst, teacher, administrator and writer was not obvious in the late 1960s. Two pivotal factors appear to have set her free on her journey. One was meeting Rowena Phillips, herself analysed by Emma Jung in Zurich. The other was doing secretarial work for Jack Kahn, a psychoanalyst, on his forthcoming book. In the event, Job's Illness: Loss, Grief and Integration was published in 1975 with an acknowledgment of Hester Solomon on the title page.

Hester Madeleine McFarland was a war baby who started life in a New Haven garage in Connecticut, later upgraded to a log cabin on a hillside, with space to roam. She was the elder of two children in the family of Emily Tutak, of Polish origin, and of Orrin McFarland, descended from a line of Scottish doctors. Despite being a top student and winning a place at university, her family could not afford to finance her, so she became a secretary in New York City. She won a scholarship to study French at Tufts. Her capacity to fill a chartered plane with fellow students bound for Paris enabled her to attend study programmes at the Sorbonne. On a hop over to London, she was introduced to a friend's brother, Jonathan, and a marriage ensued on her graduation in 1966. They had a son, Gabriel.

She was supported in her endeavours by her husband Jonathan Solomon, the brilliant Whitehall mandarin behind the highly successful privatization of British Telecom. Hester qualified as a Jungian analyst with the British Association of Psychotherapists in 1979, and as a couple therapist with the Institute of Marital Studies. She swiftly rose within the BAP Jungian stream, becoming a training analyst and assuming the chair of the Jungian analytic training. In the early 1990s she was chair of the BAP council, followed by a stint as chair of the Ethics Committee. Her administrative and political skills culminated in 2010 in the presidency, as only the second woman to hold this position, of the Zurich-based International Association for Analytical Psychology. During her term of office she unfurled the modernization of the organization's constitution and added vigour to the expansion of analytic training across the world, taking in Latin America, China, South Africa and former communist states.

Barry Watt  

Homeless people are amongst the most drastically and chronically marginalized groups in the UK. Upon coming to the attention of statutory and charitable services, they are almost invariably identified as struggling with substantial and complex physical and mental health challenges, requiring considerable medical, practical and psychological assistance. Histories of horrific sexual, physical and emotional abuse, profound neglect, criminal exploitation, precarious and substandard housing, exclusion from mainstream education, abandonment to growing up in care and repeated contact with the Criminal Justice System are just some of the many cumulative traumas homeless people routinely identify in their life experiences. Where referrals to mental health services are made, homeless folk frequently fail to meet even broad and inclusive referral criteria, their ‘needs’ generally being deemed ‘too complex’, their behaviour ‘too chaotic’ or ‘too challenging’ or their being inadmissible to therapeutic assistance due to their status as ‘dual diagnosis’, that is, actively using drugs or alcohol concurrent with one or multiple mental health diagnoses.

On the occasions homeless people do successfully access services and treatments, they all too often report that experiences of treatment frequently result in retraumatization and iatrogenic harm, instilling in them further mistrust and avoidance of ‘the system’. Drug and/or alcohol dependency, pronounced emotional dysregulation, unpredictable acting out and refusal of social norms such as accepted standards around personal hygiene or adhering to socially appropriate speech in shared spaces mark the homeless person out as a social problem and public health issue. As such, their behaviours are abnormalized, their distress pathologized. Care and treatment plans tend to be reduced to pharmacological and behavioural interventions, focused on removing or suppressing, rather than understanding or illuminating, presenting problems; a model that neatly dovetails with the moralizing of prevailing public attitudes that tends to regard the encroachment of the homeless on public spaces as a nuisance and troublesome eyesore, an offence to common decency. What mainstream public policy, social care and mental health responses to homelessness frequently fail to account for is the myriad ways in which ‘homelessness’ can function as a vital strategy of psychic survival, a dynamic solution to many profoundly complicated deadlocks and roadblocks of emotional life.

The Devil You Know is a collection of portraits divided into 11 chapters. The Introduction, Authors' Note and Coda bookend and possibly buffer the reader from some of the material within which, at its rawest, renders the book a challenging and at times, disturbing read. Written responsibly, with the lay reader in mind, this is not a textbook, but a vivid series of encounters, each one portraying an individual, each chapter named after a patient whose unique history is uncovered as we read. Most are forensic psychotherapy patients; those who have committed offences and so the naming of chapters is perhaps more significant here - as when someone enters a prison, their identity is reduced to a number which, from the outset, the authors are reminding us of the need to re-humanize by giving them names. These characters, we are told, are composites, the identities of individuals protected from the possibility of any further exploitation. As the authors point out, the relationship to a patient is ‘privileged’ in both senses of the word and so the anonymity of those who may have previously known little protection is therefore preserved.

The book, which aired on BBC Radio Four's ‘Book of the Week’, is described as a collaboration between Dr Gwen Adshead, a forensic psychotherapist and psychiatrist and the writer and dramatist Eileen Horne. As forensic psychotherapy is not usually practiced alone, and by this I am referring to the ever present ‘third’ - the criminal justice system, it is perhaps fitting that similarly, The Devil you Know is the work of more than one individual.

The cover of the book shows the image of a boy in latency, shot through a blue lens, partially obscured by the wording from the title, but the expression in the boy's unblinking eye is sadly both recognizable and compelling. It is the intense stare we encounter from patients who have experienced the legacy of severe neglect, often violence, and echoes of these feature repeatedly in the pages that follow. At the centre of each chapter, we find trauma, sometimes known, sometimes not known, at least consciously, even to the teller.

In the twentieth century, group therapy flourished in different countries. As part of The New International Library of Group Analysis, a series edited by the psychoanalyst and group analyst Earl Hopper, this book provides a cartography of Swedish

403

group therapy experiences. It is the outcome of jointly written seminars, organized by Christer Sandahl and a group of professionals in the field. It honours the work of Swedish pioneers, combining in a creative and independent way the North American and British influences, especially group analysis, on group therapy. As announced in the introduction, the aim was ‘to write an introductory book with wide applications, primarily in different forms of time-limited group therapy, and at the same time being deeply rooted in the group analytic tradition’ (p. 3). At first glance, it proposes an unexpected dialogue with different theoretical epistemologies whose combination might surprise the reader. However, its richness lies exactly in the fact that this dialogue transcends taken-for-granted theoretical and clinical frames of reference in group therapy and challenges the reader to reflect on the essence of the question ‘Why does group therapy work?‘.

In each of its 12 chapters, the authors discuss the idea of ‘group’, from early human flocks in the savannahs to the creation of family bonds, attachment and social learning, to relationships among persons with regard to the treatment of their psychological and social suffering, a moment when group therapy is fundamental. Social psychological perspectives and Kurt Lewin's ideas on the social field enabled the authors to define a group as more important than the sum of its parts/members, asserting their interaction in terms of the pursuit of common goals, for good or for evil. The idea of the group as a whole is highlighted and connected with the Foulkesian concept of ‘matrix’, defined as ‘the network of all individual mental processes, the psychological medium in which they meet, communicate and interact’ (Foulkes & Anthony, 1965, p. 26). Thus, the importance of communication and interaction conveyed by the concept of matrix inspires the authors, in Chapter 4, to explore the idea of the therapeutic group as a learning and healing environment, as a ‘space where group members can have invigorating conversations’ (p. 23).

This paper was born out of a very specific emotional experience I had with a patient that alerted me to a phenomenon of casual violence which, owing to its everydayness, may remain incipient. The experience described with Mr X is specific, but he is also a placeholder for patients who seemed to come together in my mind. The nature of this seemed both elusive and pervasive in many patients. What they seemed to have in common was a certain violence by which they were expelled from spaces - official and/or intimate. Post #MeToo, some of them were accused of being predatory. For a long time, I could not identify it in the transference. The paper traces this violence to a quotidian misogyny and furthermore to the introjection of a ‘mis-understanding link’. There appears to be a correspondence between ‘banal’ absence of thinking (Arendt, 2000) and a relationship of ‘mis-understanding’ (Bion, 1962). Such mis-understanding finds expression in forms of violent masculinity (Rose, 2021). Finally, it is suggested that contemporary masculinity is not of the older macho sort, but seems to have an affinity towards ‘adolescent states of mind’ (Meltzer, 1973). It is speculated that cultural practices seem to encourage a perpetual adolescence.

In discussion of the clinical material related to B, I was struck by the sense of unresolved mourning and impoverished contact evident both in the patient's presentation and in the relationship with the therapist themselves. It was as if there were a magnetic field around the patient preventing contact, leaving B in a state of constant hunger and dissatisfaction. While there were hints at deep and pressing states of mind that drove him at times to suicidal despair, it did not appear that these were fully presented in the consulting room, contained and digested, despite what seemed to be a safe and distant connection between the two.

We are not given much information about the patient's early life other than his rather tyrannical father, who treats him as stupid despite his clear intellectual gifts and a mother who does not protect him or acknowledge the harm his father's treatment inflicts on him, other than to offer him the means to get away, by selling her jewellery. He is ambivalent about leaving home, and is caught in an oedipal trap where he retains a sense of castration by his father, never able to become a grown man, and longing for a woman, but unable to commit to one. We learn that his mother died when he was 25, of cancer, but nothing of his feelings about this, though he engages in therapy some 20 years later. He does seem to be in a state of unresolved mourning, where, as Freud so aptly described, ‘the shadow of the ego falls on the object’ (Freud, 1917) and in the beginning of therapy he spends much time feeling suicidal and many days on his sofa, lying down. This seems an unconscious identification with a depressed or dying mother, and his internalized rage at her passing, and his father's ongoing presence, a vital and brutal force within his psyche, with obvious links to what we learn is the deadening force of ‘The Hammer’, though this is left implicit in the account. We learn that he wanted to marry ‘an American girl’ and briefly left to live abroad with her, but returned, under both parent's pressure to do so, and has been mourning this loss ever since, living in a fantasy world of what might have been, filled with regret. He has not overcome the prohibition of the father to become a sexual and independent man and returns to live in a state of unfulfilled grievance. His failure to mourn is evident in this relationship; he is in a perverse safe haven of memory and desire, without a need to actually engage in intimacy. This has a core complex flavour in which actual intimacy is avoided, telling the married woman not to leave her marriage, showing the same kind of ambivalence he has felt, as he has never really left home and despite his parents' deaths he has never really grown up.

This book represents the culmination of decades of thinking and practice by Jeanne Magagna, who has worked with some of the most difficult patients of all - those who are refusing life, nurture and emotional support through severe anorexia, self-harm and/or pervasive withdrawal.

Reading her work, one is in the humbling presence of someone who has had to dig very deep indeed in herself to find the resources to provide help to patients who are trapped within a prison of their own making, paralysed in their emotional and physical development by overwhelming fear and the need to avoid psychic pain. These patients are turning away from much more than food - many are strenuously rejecting their families and any professional offering help, and furthermore are attempting to switch off their awareness of their own emotional needs, in the grip of an omnipotent self who cannot allow the existence of the inner vulnerable and suffering child.

There are several important and impressive strands to this book. One is the deep understanding of the emotional and psychic state of these young people and of how this deadly internal situation has developed. Magagna draws on her experience of infant observation to clarify the very early and primitive roots of the anorectic young person's distress and their creation of such powerful defensive structures. Feelings of being unloved, unacceptable or unprotected as an infant engender acute pain, rage and cruel impulses which are felt to be catastrophic and impossible to express. The consequent internalized objects are imbued with sadistic and persecutory emotions, making dependency on others intolerable. The individual constructs an omnipotent self who will keep all feelings of vulnerability, need and loss out of awareness, offering addictive and potentially lethal ‘protection’ of the inner child self who is in pain and needs to be cared for. Taking the period 2015-20 as its main area of examination, the context of Danse Macabre: A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Global Dynamics is both germane to, and at times eerily prescient of, the period of turbulence, violence and flux that we are currently in. Completed as the COVID-19 pandemic was taking hold, it uses the axes of Eros/Thanatos, and of power/vulnerability to offer thoughts and associations on forces and dynamics that are at play in the world today. Although the title is of global dynamics, it is nonetheless acknowledged as being located in a post WWII European and primarily British-English perspective, though there is some reference to a broader sphere than Western Europe (particularly Eastern Europe and the Middle East). It manages to note and connect a myriad of different social movements, political activity, and national shifts over the last few years, and continually reminds the reader of the breadth and complexity of currents in the socio-political stage. It does not purport to offer answers or solutions, but sets out the often cyclical capacity for repeating mistakes and is perhaps best read as a free flowing river of ideas, that at times takes in the details of a particular landscape or the minutiae of a specific tributary.

As such, it is both an opportunity and a responsibility to be reviewing it at this moment in time. As noted, it was concluded during the pandemic and is impressive in threading the significance of this global challenge through the book - describing the impact that the spread of the virus had on social, economic and health structures. It was published not long before Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and draws attention to some of the precursors to this event, offering this somewhat chilling quote from Putin:

there are things that I believe, which should not in my position, at least, be shared with the public at large for everybody's consumption because that would look like self-advertising or a political striptease (quoted on p. 91).

Nigel Williams has contributed a warm and thoughtfully engaging book; a welcome addition to the expansion of the psychotherapeutic field of enquiry, and to psycho-social understanding of how transgenerational trauma may haunt present generations. Its warmth stems from confidence acquired through having enquired emotionally and affectively into his own ancestral field. His forebears emigrated 798 from Germany early in the twentieth century. This mixed cultural heritage grounds his observation that people of mixed national heritage, when their otherness is from the enemy state (as Germany was for the UK at the time), are likely to embody conflicted allegiances, or be perceived to. His third chapter, ‘Surveying the Literature on Multi-generational Memory’, acknowledges the many previous contributors to this subject.

So, why do ancestors and their sufferings matter in dyadic psychotherapy, when the issues in the room are so immediate and consuming? Williams' answer is that they may be in the room already, their sufferings often being spoken in the ‘I’ of patients' narratives, but as unnamed hauntings from previous generations unhappily interred in the family unconscious.

Unfortunately, there is often little psychic space in which to realize, for example, that the narratives about grandparents in war, famine, displacement or migration are signifiers from the patient's coded unconscious of hauntings or inhabitation by those forebears. These unhappy interments in the patient's unconscious call for direct recognition and to be laid to rest through processes of acceptance and reconceptualizing loss. Patients would then have more inner space in which to differentiate between what belongs to their grandparents and what is their own.

Williams writes primarily from a psycho-social perspective, with clinical implications for psychotherapy, his research consisting of in-depth interviews. His paraphrases of what interviewees told him provide the latticed groundwork for the book, underpinning his meta-narrative with the poignancy of stories discovered, told, suffered and reconceptualized.

In this study we explore the hospital care experience of women following stillbirths in an impoverished urban setting in the Western Cape Province of South Africa. A qualitative research methodology was used with the collection of primary data using the Free Association Narrative Interview Method with 10 women who experienced stillbirths at a government hospital. The study found that the women generally felt well looked after medically, but also felt an emotional disconnect from, and a need to be seen by, the medical staff. A stillbirth can confront both the woman and the clinician with their own helplessness. Without attention to the emotional needs of the staff, who seemed to be offering optimal care within their capacity, it is unlikely that the staff will be able to provide fully accessible emotional care for the women. The stories told to us by our participants suggest that more expenditure on the emotional needs of caregivers in the health system may contribute to a more emotionally accessible, sustainable workforce.

In this interview by email, Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief of the British Journal of Psychotherapy from 2009 to 2022, is in conversation with Brett Kahr, responding to questions put to her by him and the Journal's Editorial Board. The interview focuses on Scott's background and its influence on her work; her early role at Free Association Books and her role as Deputy Editor of the BJP. She identifies papers from the Journal, on her watch as Editor-in-Chief, that have resonated particularly powerfully for her, commenting that all convey a sense of urgency and immediacy. She is asked to comment on the relationship between clinical and research approaches; current debates about informed consent; the Journal's title; the impact of online as well as print publication; whether published topics have changed over time; and the Journal's international standing. She describes the editorial principles that have governed her approach to the editorship, drawing on work by Britton, Turquet, Rey and Gabbard. She comments on some challenges she has faced as an editor, and shares the highlights of her tenure. Lastly, she is asked whether the editorship has impacted on her clinical practice, whether she has any regrets, and how she would like to be remembered in relation to her editorial work.

Joanna Ryan  

This thoughtful book by a senior Jungian analyst with much experience of psychoanalytic institutions is at once timely and well overdue. Timely, because of the growing demands to challenge racism in all areas of our social life, and for white people to own and deconstruct their whiteness, rather than perpetuate racism by enacting it. Timely also because of the backlash, seen in the growing ideological and legal assaults against critical race theory and anti-racist actions. Overdue, because there pre-exists a very long history of anti-racist thought and struggle, eloquently documented in many powerful writings over centuries, and yet positive change is so slow and partial. It is especially overdue within psychoanalysis because aspects of our psychoanalytic concepts are marked by racism and there is a woeful absence of reflection and curiosity about how white hegemony is embedded and embodied in our psyches, and in our writings and trainings. Overdue also because the experiences of many black and ethnic minority trainees on our courses have been and still are those of misrecognition, discrimination and exclusion, while the whiteness of our theories and practices go unacknowledged and unproblematized. Attempts to address this within the psychoanalytic organizations of which Helen Morgan has played a leading part have been stubbornly resisted and change has been very limited, despite the growth of psychoanalytic theorizing about internalized racism.

Morgan substantially adds to the psychoanalytic literature by broadening the focus in an examination of how whiteness, as an unmarked hegemonic term, operates in and through us, socially, institutionally and personally. She shows how whiteness came to connote superiority, as an historically entrenched conscious and unconscious assumption.

This paper explores insight and the development of the thinking voice in the psychoanalytic process. It begins with music and images, narrating an important Australian historical event. The composers have created a dreaming space, and for this paper, a metaphor for the analytic space and the creative process. At once physical, aural and visual, it also exists within and reflects the patient's and analyst's shared historical and cultural frame. It is a liminal space, for exploration, crossing, and a product of the alchemy created between patient and analyst. Pickering's (2016) and Grier's (2019) consideration of musicality as an essential part of the analytic experience assists recognition of the multidimensional nature of the space created between patient and analyst. Ferro and Civitarese's (2015) conceptualization of the space where patient and analyst dream one another, and Baranger and Baranger's (2008) discussion of the bi personal field are pertinent here. Symington's idea of insight as an essential ‘thing in itself, within the individual patient helps articulation of insight as a product of an internalized linking, or parental intercourse, enabling movement to a separate third position.

Marion Milner, Psychoanalytic Technique, Winnicott, Drawing, Creativity, Pliable Medium

This article explores British psychoanalyst Marion Milner's (1900-1998) understanding of how creative play and drawing for her child and adult patients is integral to transformation in the analytic encounter. Milner explicitly proposes the act of picture-making as providing a reparative experience of an attuned, reciprocal relationship with another. Her term the ‘pliable medium’ first coined in her book On Not Being Able to Paint (1950) is explored as a concept reflective of Milner's enduring commitment to art-making as an explicitly therapeutic activity. In this way, we come to see how Milner's clinical technique depends as much on facilitating the patient's creativity in the analytic situation as it does in considering what the patient-analyst relationship can do for the patient's psychic growth.

ANALYTIC SETTING, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, EVENLY SUSPENDED ATTENTION, INTERDISCIPLINARY STUDY, MEDITATION

This paper proposes meditation as an adjunct to psychoanalytic training by adapting meditation techniques to support the development of specific internal analytic settings to fulfil established training requirements (Hinze, 2015). Previous research has suggested how established meditation techniques engender some similar states of mind to those in various psychoanalytic theories (Cooper, 1999, 2014; Epstein, 1984; Hoffer, 2020; Pelled, 2007; Rubin, 2009). Building on this work, the author develops a novel framework to describe meditation using early Buddhist principles as a foundation (Thanissaro, 2012). This framework defines how different types of concentration and discernment can be developed by using mindfulness, alertness and ardency through meditation. As far as the author is aware, this is the first time these links have been explicitly made. This is followed by the analysis of the mental qualities required for evenly suspended attention, and the development and use of a greater awareness of countertransference, chosen as they point towards the analyst's functions of external listening and internal listening respectively (Parsons, 2007). Two meditation techniques are then described within the framework, to support development of these two internal analytic settings. A clinical example shows how these techniques can be utilized in the consultation room.

On Subjectivity and the Relationship with the Other: Qualitative Results of an Interview-Study with 50 Young Muslims

Paul Kaiser PHD , Lena Barth MSc , Gonca Langbehn Dip Psy , Barbara Ruettner MD and Lutz Goetzmann MD

Lutz Goetzmann

[paul.kaiser@hafencity-institut-psychotherapie.de]

Lutz Goetzmann   Medical specialist in psychiatry and neurology, a psychotherapist and psychoanalyst habilitation at the University Hospital Zurich focusing on psychosomatic aspects of transplant medicine. She completed psychoanalytic training at the Freud Institute in Zurich and in 2011 — 20 she was head physician at the Clinic for Psychosomatic Medicine and Psychotherapy. Since 2021 she has had a private psychoanalytic practice in Berlin (IPPK). She is also co-editor of the magazine Y (magazine for atopic thinking). She has published numerous articles in the field of psychoanalytic psychosomatics.
QUALITATIVE RESEARCH, LACAN, INTERSUBJECTIVITY, INNER WORLD, IDENTITY, MUSLIM, INTEGRATION, THE BIG OTHER

The purpose of this paper is to investigate the relationship between subjectivity and the other during the course of integration among 50 young Muslims of dual national heritage in Germany. The largest group of migrants within Germany are people of Turkish and Kurdish origin. During the summer and autumn of 2018, we interviewed 50 individuals of both genders aged between 18 and 25. The interviews were carried out and evaluated in North Germany. We saw that the ‘feeling of being held’, ‘being-able-to-process-(negative)-experiences’ and ‘to take responsibility for oneself and other’ are characteristics of well-educated young Muslims. Those who feel at home in their Turkish family or in the Islamic religion are able to process positive and negative experiences and present more (mature) super-ego structures. This allows them to be able to deal with the challenges of migration and integration. Based on the data, we developed the ‘Triadic Model of Integration’ within the Lacanian L-Scheme of Subjectivity.

In 2000 I was asked to review several books published at that time on the false/recovered memory debate. These books included Memory in Dispute edited by Valerie Sinason and published in 1998. Now over 20 years later, Sinason and her co-editor

392

Ashley Conway have updated the original, with new chapters by new authors alongside some of the original authors and chapters, bringing a current perspective to their original work. It somehow brings a certain symmetry that I find myself in the fortunate position of being asked to review this current book after over two decades of working in the trauma field and having set up a specialist service for historical (non-recent) child sexual abuse (HCSA). I am also writing this in the midst of co-chairing an Expert Reference Group at the Royal College of Psychiatrists on HCSA.

In my original review I described the recovered/false memory debate and the questions it raises about truth (or falsehood) and blame. I argued then that:

Perhaps the most difficult task in all of this is to begin to think about these kinds of questions in a way that recognises the need to have facts and information and yet to allow acknowledgement of the uncertainty that one is ultimately required to hold. It is a kind of paradox: becoming better informed about the memory debate and what it has to teach us confronts us with the need to move away from a polarised position of knowing (Stubley, 2000, p. 84).

Sinason and Conway say in their introduction, referring back to the first publication in 1998: ‘Since that time, some things have changed, and others sadly remain the same’ (p. 1). This is an important, indeed pivotal, issue for this book, which brings together chapters from psychoanalysts, psychologists, researchers and survivors of childhood sexual abuse (CSA). I personally found that the most notable change was that the intervening years have lent considerable depth and weight to the views expressed.

MIRROR NEURONS, STILL FACE, THERAPEUTIC IMPASSE, ASPERGER SYNDROME, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, NEUROPSYCHOANALYSIS, COUPLE PSYCHOANALYSIS, PROJECTIVE IDENTIFICATION

The author describes how his experiencing of the husband in a neurodiverse-neurotypical couples therapy as narcissistic, led to a countertransference impasse. Using clinical material, he describes how his understanding of neuroscience helped him to view his patient as suffering from high functioning Asperger syndrome, and how this understanding helped in the resolution of the impasse. It is hoped that this clinical situation will emphasize the value of having a greater integration between our psychoanalytic and neurological understandings.

Elena Mundici

Elena Mundici

[psychotherapy.m11@gmail.com]

Elena Mundici   Psychodynamic and forensic psychotherapist registered with the British Psychoanalytic Council, the Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists and the Forensic Psychotherapy Society. Prior to embarking on psychotherapy, she trained as a classical pianist and received a MA in Piano Performance at the Milan Conservatorio Giuseppe Verdi, and an MA in Modern Literature and Musical Dramaturgy at the Universitá degli Studi in Milan. She has worked in prisons and forensic institutions both in Italy and the UK. She currently works as psychotherapy care pathway lead and adult psychotherapist at the North East London NHS Foundation Trust. She is founding partner and former director of Panoptikon. She also works in private practice. She is the treasurer of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy.
MUSIC, VIOLENCE, PRISON, BODY, SYMBOLIZATION

Many authors have explored the connection between creativity and destructiveness, and from a psychodynamic perspective both creative and destructive acts carry a psychic significance. Forensic psychotherapy, notably in the work of Estela Welldon, has shown the importance of understanding the unconscious meaning of the violent act, which can be seen as a form of communication. Similarly to violence, the execution of a piece of music involves a synergy of physical, mental and affective functions, and an interaction of conscious and unconscious forces. Reflecting on her experience of working in prison, the author explores the relationship between music and violence. Describing her work with an inmate who had committed a violent offence, the author illustrates how the structured and formal language of music provided a rigorous yet flexible space where the prisoner's internal world and unconscious phantasies could begin to be confronted. In particular, the author discusses how split off aspects connected with the index offence emerged in the ambiguous language of music. Finally, the author illustrates how the progressive acquisition of music technique can be understood as the beginning of a process of symbolization and integration.

Marco Chiesa   Fellow of the British Psychoanalytical Society and a Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists. He is Visiting Professor at the Research Department of Clinical, Education and Health Psychology, University College London, and works in private practice in London. He was Consultant Psychiatrist at the Cassel Hospital until his retirement in 2015. His main interests include treatment and management of patients with personality disorder and other challenging conditions. He has carried out a number of research projects in the area of treatment outcome for personality disorders in residential and community-based settings. He has published widely on the subject, including papers in the British Journal of Psychiatry, American Journal of Psychiatry, Journal of Personality Disorders, Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics, British Journal of Psychotherapy and International Journal of Psychoanalysis.
Depression, Self-Harm, Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Pathological Defense Organizations, False Self, Identification With the Aggressor, Psychiatric Medication

In this paper we present the main features of a 10-year, twice-weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy with a female subject (Clare) who presented with severe depression, self-harm and suicidality. Serious traumatic events in her upbringing led to the formation of a pathological defensive structure based on a rigid identification with the aggressor, used as a dysfunctional means of protecting her against the threat of severe anxiety and psychic annihilation. Although the prognosis appeared bleak, her motivation for greater self-understanding, her resilience and her therapist's commitment to analytic work allowed for a strengthening of the therapeutic alliance. Gradually and painfully, Clare succeeded in recognizing the difference between her cruel primary figures and the figure of a caring and containing psychotherapist, which in turn allowed her a more robust internalization of a benign object. The change in the nature of the transference towards greater trust coincided with improvements in her life, in the quality of her interpersonal relationship and external functioning. Psychiatric medication was gradually withdrawn and Clare found a part-time job. Improvements were maintained by follow-up consultations. The positive outcome confirms that long-term psychoanalytically oriented therapy is an effective approach for the treatment of subjects presenting with severe emotional difficulties.

Lesley Caldwell

Lesley Caldwell

[l.caldwell@ucl.ac.uk]

Lesley Caldwell  

The title of this simultaneously scholarly and deeply personal book gives some indication of its author's stance — exploratory, meditative — immediately casting the reader into a sense of an intense intertwining of author with subjects held dear in their own

197

right and in the fascination of their interrelation. Three broad areas provide the framework for Robert Snell's investigations, art in general and the art of Cézanne in particular, psychoanalysis in general and in particular its recent developments in the field theory of Nino Ferro and Giuseppe Civitarese and their concentration on Wilfred Bion, and finally, phenomenology in general and that of Merleau-Ponty and his writings on Cézanne in particular.

In following this complex series of trajectories, Snell makes ample use of quotations from these authors and their different fields of knowledge alongside his own associations to, and involvement with, each of them. This does not make for an easy read nor any definitive general argument that can necessarily be distilled easily by the reader; indeed quite a lot is asked of the reader in holding together these diverse bodies of thought in Snell's own argument.

What is notable in Snell's survey of the precursors of contemporary field theory throughout the twentieth century is the range and number of theoretical attempts to think the social and the psychological, the group and individual as irrevocably related arenas. Like every chapter in this dense book, I wanted more detail, more discussion, and more, much more of its author.

For me, this book registers its impact as a series of fragments that the reader can engage with, spin off from, pursue, or associate to, as potential starting points for personal meditation and exploration. One parallel that Snell raises on the back of a quote by Cézanne's chronicler, Joachim Gasquet, about painting and the ideas of his time is the possibly similar projects that Cézanne and Freud could be said to have been engaged in. ‘In spite of yourself you speak for your age in terms that register its most advanced awareness … Giotto answers to Dante, Tintoretto to Shakespeare, Poussin to Descartes, Delacroix to … whom’ (Gasquet, 1991, quoted in Snell, p. xv). In offering Cézanne as possibly answering to Freud, Snell says, ‘For the revolutions Cézanne and Freud started more or less at the same time were comparable in magnitude and substance; at stake were the fundamentals of how we experience the world and ourselves in it … Cézanne, like Freud, puts us in the picture and challenges our claim to mastery’ (p. xvi).

Leslie Lothstein  

The core issue in this clinical material is termination, moving from online to inperson (co-present) meetings.

218

Pauline's early life is rife with complex cumulative trauma in which conflictual attachment issues were prominent features of her underlying developmental psychopathology. This is her first session returning to the therapist's consulting room (after 16 months online due to COVID-19) with only two months left of NHS short-term in office psychotherapy. The patient cancels the first return session due to ‘illness’ (a somatic defence and a test of the therapist's will?). The therapist believed this was resistance and that the patient was using somatic illness (the patient's first line defence to avoid conflict) as an excuse and so the therapist refused the patient's request for another Zoom session, for good reason. The therapist believes that only in-person (co-presence) will allow a successful termination to take place.

Throughout treatment Pauline lived with her nuclear family (parents and younger brother) in close quarters. She experienced her father as enraged, dangerous and absent emotionally. She has a younger brother who is developmentally impaired and aggressive and has no boundaries, often bursting into her room and destroying her property. Her mother was described as withdrawn and unprotective. Pauline hates mother for not divorcing father and protecting her children. Pauline's response to the cumulative developmental trauma was to withdraw, shut down, be passive and develop somatic distress and restrictive eating. In high school she was also bullied for being overweight. According to the therapist she ‘developed an extensive list of psychosomatic symptoms which we have gradually come to understand as reflecting the damaged and fragmented state of her internal world’.

Pauline's history is consistent with Mucci's (2018) notion of someone with a ‘borderline body’, using primitive somatic defences to avoid separation. Her living situation at home (described above) was disturbing and threatening, and her primitive defensive structure and use of primitive defences immobilized her from taking action. She was experiencing what Porges (2011) called the activation of a primitive evolutionary defence of the parasympathetic dorsal vagal nerve to protect herself. Essentially, she immobilized herself and could not leave home, feel safe and be socially connected.

Sebastian Thrul

Sebastian Thrul

[sebastian.thrul@gmx.de]

Sebastian Thrul  

This book was published in the wake of the highly publicized Bell v Tavistock lawsuit, which turned on the question of whether underaged patients with gender dysphoria could consent to treatment with so-called ‘puberty blocking’ drugs. The case resulted in a decision by the United Kingdom High Court that it was highly unlikely that children under the age of 16 could be competent to consent to this form of treatment, effectively making it much more difficult for young gender dys-phoric people to get access to such medications. Susan and Marcus Evans were involved in instigating the legal proceedings against the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust, which had, in their view, adopted an approach to gender dysphoric young people that did not sufficiently explore their wish for medical interventions such as administering puberty blocking drugs or gender-related surgery. The present book aims to provide patients and clinicians with an alternative to the so-called ‘affirmative model’ of psychotherapeutic care.

After laying out their perspective on the social and political context in which the book was written, Susan and Marcus Evans provide the reader with a developmental model that considers the vicissitudes of psychosexual development leading up to and throughout adolescence that might result in a young person's wish to retreat from entering adulthood to the psychic enclave of medical transition. From the Evans' psy-choanalytically informed perspective, then, gender dysphoria is to be counted among the ‘developmental disorders that look to control ordinary developmental processes by employing primitive psychological mechanisms’ (p. 72). They argue rather convincingly for the ubiquity of psychic pain in development resulting from the ordinary demands of separation from an idealized object, of integrating the good and the bad object to a unified vision of a whole object with ambivalently perceived attributes, and of relating to the self in its less-than-perfect version. The authors describe the gender dysphoria of many of the children and young adults in the book ‘as a symptom of a fragile ego that feels threatened by conflicts and psychological pain’ (p. 240). Oftentimes, in the authors' clinical judgement, these young people lack robust enough parental care to deal with the inevitable frustrations of growing up and growing into a sexual body. Rather, the patients are described as internalizing the aggressive and hateful feelings resulting from ordinary frustrations and turning them against their own minds and bodies. At the same time, according to the authors, the possibility of subjugating, manipulating and changing the sexual body provides these young people with a powerful sense of being able to recreate an idealized version of the self after all.

This paper explores psychoanalytic definitions of creativity and presents a creatively relational approach working with clients presenting with cultural issues and illustrates this with a clinical example. The author explores her personal and historical contribution to the countertransferential elements of this article using the autobiographical and ethnographical to examine the emergence of and dependence on creativity. Linking the arts and psychoanalysis, she elucidates the relationship between what is personal and what is political and asks the audience as they read to keep considering what might be personal for them. She reviews concepts of Winnicott and Klein's creative in psychological terms; that of an active demonstration of the ego being different from the creative as the production of an object, the commonality being the creation of a new stimulus. She considers a case example from a socio-genetic perspective to demonstrate the creative as a response to trauma. Holding the view that an urgent need and therapeutic responsibility exists for new creative measures she concludes that it is in the articulation of the therapist's unconscious psychic reality where the potential lies to actively acknowledge and avoid the deepening of existing societal fissures.
